title: Large-deviations theory for growing chemical reaction networks
authors: Praful Gagrani, Ignacio Madrid, Tetsuya J Kobayashi
abstract: Growing biochemical systems are intrinsically noisy, with one important source of stochasticity arising from the discrete reaction events of the underlying biochemical network. Because growing systems do not generally admit stationary abundance distributions, it is unclear how to separate this intrinsic chemical noise from other sources of variability in population and single-cell data. Here we develop a large-deviation theory for exponentially growing stochastic chemical reaction networks by decomposing abundance into volume and composition. In these coordinates, balanced growth corresponds to a stable composition together with exponentially increasing volume. We show that composition fluctuations satisfy a large-deviation principle with speed equal to the volume of the growing system, and the corresponding quasipotential is selected by a solution of the contact Hamilton--Jacobi equation. We also derive a fluctuation theory for accumulated observables and show that their covariances decay with accumulated-volume, rather than with physical time. Applications to a minimal autocatalytic network and a coarse-grained cellular growth model demonstrate how the theory predicts composition quasipotentials, growth-rate fluctuations, and correlations between observables. The framework therefore provides a stochastic null model for single-cell heterogeneity generated by the intrinsic stochasticity of the underlying chemical reaction network.
summary: This paper establishes a rigorous large-deviation theory for stochastic chemical reaction networks that undergo exponential growth. It decomposes the system state into volume and composition, showing that composition fluctuations are governed by a quasipotential. The theory provides a powerful stochastic null model for interpreting single-cell heterogeneity in biochemical systems.
main_problem: Developing a large-deviation and fluctuation theory for stochastic Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) operating in a growing, non-stationary regime.
main_result: The composition fluctuations satisfy a large-deviation principle governed by a quasipotential derived from a contact Hamilton-Jacobi equation, and observable covariances decay with accumulated-volume.
method: The theory decomposes the stochastic abundance into volume and composition coordinates, utilizing large-deviation theory and variational methods.
model_or_system: The model is a stochastic CRN, exemplified by a coarse-grained cellular growth model, where the state is tracked by normalized abundance, volume, and composition.
key_observables: Composition quasipotential, growth-rate fluctuations, and covariances of accumulated-volume-averaged observables.
important_parameters: The system operates in a supercritical, exponentially growing regime ($\Lambda > 0$), with the fluctuation speed scaling with the accumulated volume.
main_assumptions: The system exhibits balanced growth, and the reaction rates are assumed to be homogeneous functions of degree one (scalable).
figures_summary: Figures show empirical quasipotential collapse under volume scaling and confirm the predicted decay scaling for covariances using accumulated-volume estimators.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the setup, develops the large-deviation theory for composition fluctuations, and then applies the framework to analyze the moments and covariances of accumulated-volume-averaged observables.
why_interesting: While focused on chemical kinetics, the mathematical machinery—large deviations, Hamilton-Jacobi equations, and fluctuation theorems—is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics in open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Abundance and composition dynamics for the two-species autocatalytic network. We simulated 2000 stochastic trajectories with system-scale parameter K = 101, initialized at (nA, nB) = (59, 42). The abundance variables and total volume grow exponentially, while the composition remains near the attracting balanced-growth composition. The composition variance decreases as the volume grows.

FIG. 2: Composition distributions and quasipotential for the two-species autocatalytic network. The left panel shows composition probability densities at increasing volumes or nominal balanced-growth times. The right panel shows the empirical quasipotential, −log(PDF)/(Kv), overlaid with the solution of Eq. (36). Solid curves correspond to fixed-volume sampling; dotted curves correspond to physical-time sampling. Their close agreement in this example indicates that volume fluctuations are subleading for the displayed compositions and times.

FIG. 3: Variances and covariance of the accumulated-volume-averaged observables in Eq. (36). The variance and covariance at each time t are scaled by the deterministic accumulated-volume level a⋆ t = v0(eΛt −1)/Λ. The theoretical predictions are obtained from the Hessian of the SCGF ηθ. An approximation using the Hessian of the fixed point energy Eθ is also shown.

Figure 4 shows the same fluctuations without rescal- ing and compares them with the conventional time- averaged estimators defined in Sec. II D. Both averag- ing schemes approach the same balanced-growth means, but their variances have different asymptotic behavior. The accumulated-volume estimators weight later times more strongly, when the system is larger and more re- action events are observed, and their covariances decay on the scale 1/(KAt). In the simulations this leads to substantially smaller long-time fluctuations than for the corresponding time-averaged estimators.

FIG. 4: Fluctuations of composition and growth-rate estimators in the two-species autocatalytic network. Accumulated-volume-averaged estimators are compared with the theoretical covariance prediction and with the corresponding conventional time-averaged estimators. Both averaging schemes converge to the same balanced-growth means, but their fluctuations decay differently: the accumulated-volume estimators decay on the accumulated-volume scale, whereas the time-averaged estimators decay O(t−1) in physical time. For the parameters shown, the accumulated-volume estimators consequently attain smaller variances at long times.
